newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Seventeen detained after riot on Indonesia's Java.
newsitem.headline: Seventeen detained after riot on Indonesia's Java.

text.p: Indonesian authorities detained 17 people in a Java town after recent riots, apparently sparked by reports that a popular singer had switched political allegiances, the Media Indonesia daily reported on Thursday.

The newspaper quoted the army chief of Central Java province Major-General Soebagyo as saying on Wednesday that there was no loss of life in the rioting which flared on Tuesday night in Pekalongan, a coastal town 300 km (190 miles) east of Jakarta.
The rioters mainly attacked the property of ethnic Chinese.
"These 17 people will be processed according to the law and the results cannot be released as we are still in the investigation phase," Soebagyo was quoted as saying.
It was the first violence in Java since a mob attacked Chinese homes and businesses, Christian churches and Buddhist temples in the town of Tasikmalaya in western Java in January.
Four people died in those riots, set off by an incident of police brutality against a Moslem teacher.
Ethnic disturbances between local Dayaks and immigrant Madurese also rocked West Kalimantan province on Borneo island last month. At least 12 people died, military officials and residents said.
Residents said on Thursday they knew of no fresh rioting overnight but the scars of Tuesday's violence -- looted shops and burnt houses and cars -- were still evident.

Police in Pekalongan were not immediately available for comment. Media Indonesia said six shops had been looted and that three motorcylces and one car were burnt. It did not mention any damage to houses.
"A number of houses belonging to the Chinese have been either damaged or burned," a Chinese man told Reuters by phone from Pekalongan on Wednesday.
"It seems that the target is the Chinese even though they have nothing to do with what has happened," another resident said.
The official Antara news agency quoted army chief General Hartono as describing the violence on Wednesday as stemming from a singer's apparent switch of political allegiances.

Popular pop singer Rhoma Irama appeared at a ceremony of the ruling Golkar party in Pekalongan on Tuesday along with a high-profile television Islamic preacher and President Suharto's eldest daughter Siti Hardiyanti Rukmana.
"They used to see Rhoma as a member of one of the existing political parties and now they see that Rhoma has switched to another party," Hartono said.
Irama in the past backed the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) but is now listed as a candidate in the country's May 29 poll as a member of Golkar.
The only three parties permitted to contest the elections are Golkar, the PPP and the Indonesian Democratic Party.
